title: Evaluating ChatGPT-4 Vision on Brazil's National Undergraduate Computer Science Exam
source_used: arXiv preprint 2406.09671v1 (oa_url); author-accepted version of the ACM TOCE article
ft_reason: HE computing (Brazilian BCS national exam); evaluates a GenAI model on a real high-stakes assessment, which directly informs exam vulnerability; peer reviewed (ACM TOCE); 2024; English.
redesign_note: Shows a multimodal LLM scoring in the top 10% on a real national CS exam, including visual and open questions, so exam formats assumed to resist AI are vulnerable.
study_design: Experimental evaluation of an LLM on a real exam (zero-shot chain-of-thought prompting, reassessment step, independent expert panel review of disagreements)
level: Undergraduate (Bachelor in Computer Science, national exit exam ENADE 2021)
sample: ENADE 2021 BCS specific-knowledge component: 3 open questions and multiple-choice questions (19 scored, 6 excluded by the exam's own psychometrics); human reference group of 10,119 participants from over 300 institutions (Sec 3.1)
genai_tools: ChatGPT-4 Vision (answering); ChatGPT-4 Turbo (reflection on performance)

key_findings.finding: ChatGPT-4 Vision reached a final weighted score of 66.3 against a participant mean of 36.7, placing it in the top 10 percentile of exam takers.
On open questions it averaged 54.2/100 (participant mean 15.2), in the top 8 percentile; on 19 scored multiple-choice items it scored 68.4% correct.
It answered 75.0% of questions with visual elements correctly versus 63.6% of text-only questions, so image-based items did not protect against the model.
Accuracy fell as item difficulty rose (100% Easy to 0% Very Hard), and its errors came from question interpretation, logical reasoning and visual acuity.
Expert review of disagreements exposed vague or ambiguous exam questions; the author suggests LLMs could be used to pre-test exam items.

dimensions.capability_verification: A current multimodal LLM outperforms most candidates on a national CS exam, so exam scores may not verify human capability where AI access is possible.
dimensions.integrity_security: Multimodal (image-based) questions do not resist GenAI; the model did better on visual than on text-only items.
dimensions.feasibility: Running exam items through an LLM before administration is proposed as a practical check of question quality.

author_recommendations: Use multimodal LLMs to test and refine exam questions before administration, to detect ambiguity (not tested)
Keep human oversight to verify model accuracy and protect fairness in high-stakes exams (not tested)
Future work: compare other multimodal models, use repeated attempts and advanced prompting (not tested)
limitations: Single run per question with zero-shot CoT prompts; one model family only; no traditional exam-validation benchmark; Portuguese exam translated for reporting; a single exam year (Sec 6.3).

quality.note: Clear RQs, transparent procedure with open materials, explicit limitations; the evidence is about AI capability rather than student behaviour.

title: The Pedagogical Fit Of Generative Artificial Intelligence: Rethinking Assessment And Learning In Higher Education
venue: The American Journal of Engineering And Technology
ft_reason: Amendment 3: a theoretical synthesis of GenAI adoption (task-technology fit, TAM/UTAUT); it argues summative assessment is misaligned with GenAI but proposes no specific redesign and gives no evidence on assessment vulnerability, so it is c_not_redesign.
redesign_note: Offers only a general claim that GenAI fits formative feedback well and summative assessment poorly; no design is proposed or evaluated.
study_design: Conceptual / theoretically integrative qualitative synthesis (no primary data)
sample: No primary data; a 'reference corpus' of studies and reports, with no stated search strategy or number of sources (Sec 2)

key_findings.finding: The synthesis argues GenAI fits formative tasks such as feedback and drafting well, but fits summative assessment poorly because the tool can perform the task being measured.
Fit is said to differ by discipline: computing and engineering students see GenAI as a legitimate aid, while humanities settings are more sceptical.
An analogy with AI-driven behaviour-driven test automation is used to argue that AI should run human-defined criteria rather than generate the assessed work.

dimensions.integrity_security: Argues that letting GenAI produce assessable outputs makes summative assessment invalid; no data.
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Argues for AI use in formative and feedback roles rather than for producing assessed outputs.

author_recommendations: Use GenAI for formative feedback and scaffolding rather than for producing summative outputs (not tested)
Extend acceptance models with task legitimacy and academic integrity constructs (not tested)
limitations: Secondary synthesis with no reported search or selection method; relies on self-reported survey literature and rests heavily on one software-testing analogy; acknowledged as quickly dated (Sec 2, Sec 4).

quality.note: Conceptual paper; the corpus is not described and the claims are only loosely tied to cited evidence.

title: Academic integrity surrounding the use of generative AI in higher education: Lenses from ICT college students
ft_reason: Amendment 3: a qualitative study of ICT students' perceptions of GenAI and academic integrity; it offers attitudes and perceptions only, with no assessment design and no evidence of actual use on assessed work, so it is c_not_redesign.
redesign_note: Student views that schools and teachers should set rules for when AI use is acceptable; nothing about how to redesign assessment.
study_design: Exploratory qualitative study; semi-structured interviews; thematic analysis
sample: 30 ICT students from several universities in Eastern Visayas, chosen by purposive and convenience sampling; one-on-one recorded interviews (Sec 3.2-3.4)
genai_tools: Generative AI in general; ChatGPT shown as an example (Figure 1)

key_findings.finding: Students saw GenAI as helpful for generating ideas, speeding up work and giving support in ICT learning.
Students named overreliance, dishonesty (copying AI output into assignments unchanged) and learning insufficiency as the main integrity risks.
Students wanted schools to set clear AI-use rules, including citation and acceptable AI input, and teachers to explain where use becomes misuse.
key_findings.location: Sec 4, Objective 3 themes (Role of Schools; Role of Teachers)

dimensions.integrity_security: Students perceive that peers copy AI-generated content into assignments without changes (perception only).
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Students ask for institutional and teacher guidance that defines acceptable AI use and citation.

author_recommendations: Institutions should adopt structured guidelines and policies for responsible GenAI use (not tested)
Educators should integrate discussion of ethics and critical thinking about AI into teaching (not tested)
limitations: Small purposive sample of Filipino ICT students only; perceptions captured at an early stage of GenAI adoption; analysis procedure briefly described (Sec 6).

quality.note: Adequate small qualitative study, but the analytic procedure and reflexivity are thinly reported.

title: Generative AI Adoption and Self-Reported Academic Integrity Risk: A Student Taxonomy in Latin American Higher Education
authors: Juan Carlos Torres-Díaz; Diana Rivera; Ana María Beltrán Flandoli
source_used: OpenAlex abstract (abstract_inverted_index); the MDPI full text and PDF returned HTTP 403 (bot protection), and no repository copy was found
ft_reason: Amendment 3: a survey taxonomy of general GenAI adoption and self-reported delegation tendency; it is not about assessed work or assessment design, so it is c_not_redesign (general adoption). Decided from the abstract only.
redesign_note: Gives adoption profiles and self-reported intellectual delegation, which could at most inform differentiated AI literacy; there is no assessment-specific evidence.
study_design: Quantitative cross-sectional survey; k-means cluster analysis
sample: 3415 students from eight Ecuadorian public universities, quota-balanced by discipline (abstract)
genai_tools: GenAI across text, mathematics, programming, image and music generation (abstract)

key_findings.finding: Clustering on five multimodal use variables gave four profiles: Passive 44.3%, Artist 24.4%, Technical 18.3% and Comprehensive 13%.
Profile membership was associated with discipline (chi2 = 517.85; Cramer's V = 0.225).
The Comprehensive profile reported the highest self-reported intellectual delegation to AI (eta2 = 0.114); the authors link ethical risk to whether outputs are directly presentable.

dimensions.integrity_security: Self-reported delegation to AI varies by user profile, suggesting integrity risk is unevenly distributed (abstract only).

author_recommendations: Differentiate AI literacy programmes and institutional governance by student profile (not tested)
limitations: Abstract only. Self-reported cross-sectional data from one country; limitations could not be checked against the full text.

quality.note: Abstract only; the design and sample look sound but the analysis and limitations could not be checked.

title: Java academic benchmark: Exam-based evaluation of LLMs on object-oriented programming
authors: Alessio Cocchieri; Luca Ragazzi; Gianluca Aguzzi; Giacomo Frisoni; Lorenzo Molfetta; Gianluca Moro
source_used: OpenAlex abstract; publisher PDF (hybrid OA, CC BY) and the ScienceDirect page returned HTTP 403/bot check; no arXiv or repository copy found
ft_reason: HE computing (bachelor OOP exams); evaluates 27 LLMs on 103 authentic university Java exams, which directly informs how vulnerable programming exams are to GenAI; peer reviewed (JSS); 2026; English. Abstract is substantive enough to extract.
redesign_note: Shows that large closed LLMs match or beat bachelor-level students on a decade of real Java OOP exams, especially when used agentically with compiler and test feedback.
study_design: Benchmark construction and evaluation of LLMs (execution-based JUnit scoring plus an LLM-as-a-Judge framework, KODE)
discipline: Computer Science / Software Engineering (object-oriented programming in Java)
sample: 103 authentic Java exams collected over a decade at one large university, with 506 expert-written JUnit tests; 27 LLMs evaluated (abstract)
genai_tools: 27 LLMs (open and closed models; not named in abstract)

key_findings.finding: Larger closed LLMs matched or exceeded bachelor-level students on authentic OOP exam tasks, especially in agentic mode with compiler and test feedback.
Smaller open models lagged behind students.
The class-level design exposed recurring OOP misconceptions in model outputs; a separate LLM judge (KODE) scored OOP adherence on four pedagogical dimensions.

dimensions.capability_verification: Real programming exam tasks can be solved by frontier LLMs at or above student level, so unsupervised code submissions do not verify capability (abstract only).
dimensions.integrity_security: Agentic use (iterating with compiler and test feedback) further raises LLM success on exam tasks (abstract only).

author_recommendations: not reported (abstract only)
limitations: Abstract only; results are 'under our evaluation protocol' from one university's exams; limitations could not be checked against the full text.

quality.note: Abstract only; a large, transparent benchmark with Open Science validation, but the details could not be checked.

title: STEM exam performance: Open‐ versus closed‐book methods in the large language model era
authors: Rasi Mizori; Muhayman Sadiq; Malik Takreem Ahmad; Anthony Siu; Reubeen Rashid Ahmad; Zijing Yang
source_used: PubMed Central copy PMC11663729 via Europe PMC render (the Wiley pdfdirect link was blocked)
ft_reason: HE STEM (mostly health sciences; partial computing relevance); compares open-book and closed-book exam formats and discusses LLM-era validity at length; peer-reviewed systematic review with meta-analysis; 2024; English. Included because the format evidence and the LLM-era recommendations inform exam redesign, although the included studies predate LLMs.
redesign_note: Meta-analytic evidence that open-book exams give higher marks and may measure different competencies, plus an untested proposal for a hybrid AI-open then closed-book exam.
study_design: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis (PRISMA; Newcastle-Ottawa risk of bias)
country: UK (review team); included studies from USA (5), UK (2), Saudi Arabia (1)
sample: 8 studies (searched in PubMed, Scopus and ERIC, Feb-May 2023; English, 2013 onwards); all single-institution (Sec 2, Sec 3.1)
genai_tools: LLMs in general (GPT-3, ChatGPT) discussed; none used in included studies

key_findings.finding: Open-book exams gave higher marks than closed-book exams (mean difference 5.91, 95% CI 2.79 to 9.04), with very high heterogeneity (I2 = 97%).
The effect held in both observational (MD 6.89) and quasi-experimental (MD 3.79) subgroups, with no significant subgroup difference.
Included studies reported proctoring effects, technical problems and cheating in online exams; varying the questions was used to reduce cheating.
All included studies predate widespread LLMs; the authors argue that unproctored open-book recall questions are especially exposed to LLM score inflation.

dimensions.authenticity: Open-book exams are argued to reflect real-world information access, but LLMs may erode that authenticity advantage.
dimensions.capability_verification: LLMs could inflate open-book scores without deep understanding, which undermines what the exam verifies.
dimensions.integrity_security: Unproctored open-book formats are flagged as most exposed to unchecked AI use; proctoring or restrictions are suggested.
dimensions.lo_alignment: Open-book and closed-book exams are inferred to assess different competencies, so the choice of format should follow intended outcomes.
dimensions.feasibility: Open-book exams cut invigilation cost, but they need secure platforms, faculty training and technical support.
dimensions.accessibility_equity: The authors call for equitable access to the technology that advanced test formats need.

author_recommendations: Use closed-book or AI-restricted invigilated formats for short-answer and recall questions (not tested)
Reserve open-book formats for long-answer, higher-order questions (not tested)
A hybrid exam: a timed phase with AI and internet access to gather information, then a closed-book synthesis phase (not tested)
Research the integrity of open-book exams with respect to AI use (not tested)
limitations: Only 8 heterogeneous single-institution studies from three countries, all before LLMs; I2 = 97%; LLM implications are speculative (Sec 4.1).

quality.note: Sound review method; the GenAI conclusions go beyond the pre-LLM evidence.

title: Rethinking Assessment for Engineering Students in Higher Education in the Age of Generative AI: A Critical Narrative Review
venue: Asian Journal of Education and Social Studies
source_used: OpenAlex abstract; the publisher PDF (journalajess.com) and HAL copies (hal-05738214, hal-05747639) were behind bot-check pages, which were not bypassed
ft_reason: HE engineering assessment redesign for GenAI; proposes an assessment architecture (Dual-Assurance) drawing on a dated literature search; peer-reviewed journal; 2026; English. Abstract is detailed enough to extract.
redesign_note: Proposes a Dual-Assurance Assessment Architecture: protected evidence of independent competence plus AI-integrated evidence of professional judgement, triangulated through staged work, orals, live demonstration and provenance.
study_design: Critical narrative review (literature 1 Jan 2018 to 27 Jun 2026)
sample: Literature published 1 January 2018 to 27 June 2026 plus earlier foundational work; number of sources not reported in abstract
genai_tools: General-purpose and specialised GenAI/AI systems (not named)

key_findings.finding: Neither blanket prohibition nor unrestricted adoption is a defensible general approach; authenticity alone is insufficient because realistic take-home tasks stay open to undisclosed AI help.
The review proposes separating protected evidence of independent competence (threshold and safety-relevant skills) from AI-integrated evidence of professional judgement.
Evidence should be triangulated through staged work, oral explanation, live demonstration, provenance and programme-level assessment mapping.
AI detectors are judged too unreliable and potentially inequitable to serve as stand-alone evidence of misconduct; AI-assisted grading needs human oversight.

dimensions.authenticity: Authentic take-home tasks are not enough on their own because they stay open to undisclosed AI use.
dimensions.capability_verification: Calls for protected evidence of independent competence for threshold and safety-relevant capabilities.
dimensions.integrity_security: Detectors are too unreliable to serve as stand-alone evidence of misconduct.
dimensions.lo_alignment: Reform should focus on the validity of inferences about student capability, with programme-level assessment mapping.
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: AI-integrated tasks are proposed where responsible tool use is itself an intended learning outcome.
dimensions.process_visibility: Staged work and provenance are proposed as evidence alongside the final product.
dimensions.accessibility_equity: Detector inequity is flagged as a concern.

author_recommendations: Adopt a Dual-Assurance Assessment Architecture, presented as an evidence-derived organising model rather than a validated framework (not tested)
Triangulate staged work, oral explanation, live demonstration and provenance (not tested)
Do not use AI detectors as stand-alone evidence of misconduct (not tested)
limitations: Abstract only. A narrative (not systematic) review; the authors say the architecture is not validated; full-text limitations could not be checked.

quality.note: Abstract only; the explicit statement that the model is unvalidated counts as an acknowledged limitation.

title: A Hybrid LLM-Optimized Framework for Autonomous Viva Assessment Using Retrieval Augmented Generation and Prompt Engineering
authors: Dhanushka Balasingham; Jaliya L. Wijayaraja; Chathurangika Kahandawaarachchi; Nuwan Kodagoda
source_used: IEEE Access publisher PDF (gold OA, CC BY) via the Crossref full-text link (ieeexplore ielx8, arnumber 11683425)
ft_reason: HE computing (4th-year IoT module); implements and evaluates an LLM-based system that generates personalised viva questions from each student's submission and scores the answers; peer reviewed; 2026; English. Borderline under Amendment 3, because it is partly an AI-grading tool and is framed by workload and examiner bias rather than GenAI integrity. Coded a_redesign because it evaluates a scalable oral-assessment design.
redesign_note: Evaluates a way to scale viva voce assessment with LLM-generated, submission-specific questions and automated scoring; relevant to oral verification at scale, though not framed as an integrity response.
study_design: Design science / system development with comparative evaluation against human grading and alternative prompting methods
discipline: Computing (Internet of Things module, Faculty of Computing, SLIIT)
sample: Over 250 students in 67 groups; 670 viva question-answer pairs; 200 generated questions for comparing methods; 160 manually graded responses from 4 examiners; 50 feedback triplets reviewed by an expert (Sec III-C)
genai_tools: ChatGPT as the underlying LLM, with LangChain, FAISS and RAG; ChatGPT, Claude, Grok and Gemini compared for variability

key_findings.finding: The hybrid method (prompt engineering, RAG and few-shot calibration) produced the most relevant questions: 74.3% relevance to the assignment and 66.6% to the student's proposal.
Hybrid dynamic prompting reached QWK 0.782 agreement with human grades, a 29.9% improvement over static prompting, with 89.57% mark-distribution overlap.
Variability across four LLMs (CoV 8.44%) was much lower than among human examiners (CoV 32.69%).
Generated feedback had 92.0% expert agreement, but the system sometimes asked students to repeat answers already given to linked questions.

dimensions.capability_verification: Viva questions tied to each student's own project are generated and scored automatically, supporting oral checks of understanding.
dimensions.lo_alignment: Questions are grounded in assignment content and the student's submission through RAG.
dimensions.scalability: Designed to scale viva assessment as enrolment grows; tested with over 250 students in 67 groups.
dimensions.workload: Motivated by the examiner hours vivas need; at least two evaluators per session under the current practice (Sec III-B, Figure 4).
dimensions.feasibility: Implemented with Streamlit, LangChain, FAISS and ChatGPT; currently text-only, without the planned avatar or speech interface.

author_recommendations: Add an avatar-based front end with speech-to-text for spoken viva interaction (not tested)
Add memory of earlier answers so linked questions are not re-asked (not tested)
Extend to other modules and LLM architectures (not tested)
limitations: One module at one institution; text-only interaction; feedback errors on connected questions; small expert-review subsets; not evaluated for integrity or GenAI-misuse outcomes (Sec VI).

quality.note: Well-reported system evaluation; its relevance to secure assessment is indirect.

title: Guidelines for Integrating Generative AI Into Programming Education at The Diploma Level in Malaysian Polytechnics: Balancing Benefits and Risks
authors: WAN SALMIZI WAN MAHMOOD; Nor Farahwahida Mohd Noor; NIK RAHAYA NIK ISHAK
ft_reason: Tertiary (diploma-level polytechnic) programming education; proposes guidelines that explicitly include assessment redesign (live coding, oral defences, debugging exercises) and AI-use citation; peer-reviewed journal; 2025; English.
redesign_note: A guideline framework, validated in focus groups, that recommends live coding assessments, oral defences, debugging exercises and AI-citation rules in programming courses.
study_design: Qualitative multi-phase guideline development: systematic literature review (15 papers), semi-structured interviews, focus groups
sample: 15 papers in the SLR; 10 programming instructors interviewed (purposive); 2 focus groups with 5 educators and 5 students (Methodology)
genai_tools: Generative AI in general (no specific tools named)

key_findings.finding: Instructors found AI-assisted work hard to assess because AI code looks well structured and error-free; some had already added oral explanations and debugging exercises.
key_findings.location: Results and Discussion: Insights from Semi-Structured Interviews

key_findings.finding: In focus groups, students admitted relying on AI without fully understanding its code, and educators backed the redesigned assessment methods in the guidelines.
key_findings.location: Results and Discussion: Validation from FGDs

key_findings.finding: The guidelines tell educators to redesign assessments with live coding, oral defences and debugging exercises, and tell institutions to define acceptable AI use and require AI citation.

dimensions.capability_verification: Live coding, oral defences and debugging exercises are proposed to check genuine comprehension.
dimensions.integrity_security: Educators report difficulty telling student effort from AI assistance in submitted code.
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: Students should attempt problems before using AI, and should cite and modify AI-generated code; institutions should define acceptable use.
dimensions.feasibility: Focus groups judged the guidelines practical; AI literacy training for staff is seen as a prerequisite.
dimensions.process_visibility: Process-based evaluation is named as a future assessment direction.

author_recommendations: Redesign programming assessments with live coding, oral defences and debugging exercises (not tested)
Institutions should define acceptable and unacceptable AI use and require citation of AI-generated code (not tested)
Make AI literacy training mandatory for educators and students (not tested)
Pilot the guidelines and run controlled and longitudinal trials (not tested)
limitations: Small qualitative samples; the SLR method is thinly reported; the guidelines are validated only by perception in focus groups and not piloted; limitations are not discussed explicitly beyond future-research needs.

quality.note: Clear aim and mixed qualitative design, but the analysis is thinly reported and there is no limitations section.

title: Analysis of Generative Artificial Intelligence Governance in Publicly Available Documentation of Global and Saudi Universities Offering Health Informatics Programs
venue: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
source_used: Dove Medical Press publisher PDF (OpenAlex location for DOI 10.2147/AMEP.S632635; the queue had no DOI and the DOAJ record has no full-text link)
ft_reason: Amendment 3: a comparative analysis of published institutional GenAI governance documents; it covers policy content, not an assessment design or evidence on assessment vulnerability, use on assessed work, or policy outcomes, so it is c_not_redesign.
redesign_note: Reports how often university policies cover assessment governance and disclosure, which is useful policy context but not evidence for redesign.
study_design: Qualitative document analysis and comparative policy analysis (directed content analysis, nine domains; Fisher's exact tests)
country: Saudi Arabia and 30 international universities (North America, Europe, Asia, Australia)
sample: 46 universities (30 international chosen via QS 2025 subject rankings; 16 Saudi); 117 public governance sources (111 international, 6 Saudi), retrieved March-May 2026; inter-coder kappa 0.96 (Methods)

key_findings.finding: All 30 international universities had public GenAI governance, against 6 of 16 Saudi universities (37.5%).
Assessment Governance was covered by 72.1% of international and 66.7% of Saudi sources; Academic Integrity by 86.5% and 66.7%.
Transparency and Disclosure (87.4% vs 33.3%, p = 0.005) differed most; international sources more often required students to disclose and cite AI use.

dimensions.integrity_security: Academic integrity provisions appear in most sources; Saudi sources focus on discipline and monitoring.
dimensions.appropriate_ai_use: International policies more often combine acceptable-use rules with disclosure, human oversight and approved platforms; Saudi sources stress sanctions.

author_recommendations: Universities without formal GenAI governance should publish institution-wide policies covering transparency, disclosure, ethics and AI literacy (not tested)
Accreditation bodies should add discipline-specific AI-governance expectations to Health Informatics programme standards (not tested)
limitations: Public documents only, so internal policy and actual practice are not captured; only six Saudi sources; the maturity score is not validated.

quality.note: Rigorous document analysis with reliability testing; out of scope for assessment redesign.
